title: RagnaDuds - Private Ragnarok Online Server
description: A rathena server built for friends split between Denmark and Brazil. Multi-arch Docker images on an ARM cloud VM, a patched and translated 32 bit game client, installers for Windows and Linux, and a retro website with live server stats. You can check it live [here](https://ragnaduds.duckdns.org)!
content:
Ragnarok Online was the game of my childhood. My friends are now spread between Denmark and Brazil, which is a terrible setup for nostalgia, so instead of hunting for a public server we could all agree on, I built us our own. Two of them actually, one for the classic pre-renewal era we played as kids and one for the modern renewal era, plus a website, installers for Windows and Linux, and a small command line tool so I can run the whole thing from my kitchen table.

It is friends only and non commercial. Honestly, the game part was never the hard part. What kept me busy for weeks was everything around it, the infrastructure, the packaging, and a frankly unreasonable amount of reverse engineering on a client that was compiled when I was still in school.

![Prontera, the capital, rendered by the browser client](/images/ragnaduds-prontera.mp4)

## How it runs

Everything lives on one ARM VM from Oracle Cloud, twelve containers behind a single compose file. rathena, the open source C++ emulator, needs three processes per server (login, char, map), plus a small web api that newer clients expect, plus its own MariaDB. Two eras, so double all of that, then Caddy in front and a status sidecar watching both.

::flow ragnaduds

Three decisions made the rest of the project boring in the good way, which is exactly what I want from something I maintain on a Tuesday night.

- **Images are built once on my PC**, for amd64 and arm64, then pushed to a private registry. The VM never sees a line of source code, it only pulls.
- **Configs never go into an image or into git.** Each host has its own folder with secrets, rates, game scripts, mounted at runtime. Changing a drop rate needs no rebuild.
- **The databases have no public port.** Only the game containers and the sidecar reach them, over internal docker networks.

![The stack running on my machine, from the same compose file as the VM](/images/ragnaduds-docker.png)

## The command center

One Bash script wraps all of it. I wrote it because I got tired of remembering which flag went where at one in the morning, and it ended up being the piece I use the most.

- `release` builds multi arch, pushes, tags both latest and the git sha, so a rollback is a tag change instead of a rebuild
- `up vm` rsyncs the configs, pulls, recreates only what actually changed, warns me first if somebody is playing right now
- `start` and `stop` run only the era we picked for that night
- `accounts` applies the local accounts file over ssh as idempotent SQL
- `package` and `files` build the client zips and upload them resumably
- `backup` pulls database dumps down to my PC, with a cron on the VM keeping seven days

::flow ragnaduds-release

## The client was the hard part

The server is a modern codebase. You compile it, you move on. The client is a 32 bit Windows program from another era, running under Wine for me and natively for my friends, and it very much does not want to talk to anything it was not born to talk to.

The exe build date has to match the server packet version exactly, so I picked a 2021 Korean exe for the classic server, a 2026 one for renewal, then compiled each server for its date. Both exes went through **WARP**, an open source patcher, to read local files before the game archives, drop the anti cheat, point at our address. Those patch sessions are version controlled like everything else. Along the way I wrote a small Python reader for the GRF archive format so I could actually see what the client was loading instead of guessing.

::flow ragnaduds-client

The one I am proud of is the item table. The 2026 exe only ever loads a single compiled Lua file full of Korean names, and the English translation just sits in the same folder being politely ignored. So that file became a tiny loader that runs the original bytecode, overlays the English table on top of it, then appends our custom items. Testing it meant building a **32 bit Lua container**, because the bytecode is 32 bit and nothing modern would even parse it. Twenty seven thousand items load in half a second.

The cash shop bug was more fun to hunt. The first item showed the right price, the second one showed 544194803. The exe had been patched to expect item preview data in every shop entry, the server was not sending it, so every entry after the first was read out of alignment. One compile flag in the Dockerfile fixed it, with rathena's source untouched.

## Bringing a dead server back

Brazil's official server shut down in 2026 and my Brazilian friends would not stop talking about its events. So I went digging in the Wayback Machine, found the old announcements, matched Portuguese monster names to ids through community databases, and rebuilt three of them.

- **Mapas Especiais**, eight rooms with instant respawn and no experience loss
- **Cheffenia**, an MVP arena with doubled boss HP and a thousand kill daily fatigue
- **Turn In**, a hunting quest

The special maps are shared instances, private copies of existing maps reachable only through the event NPCs, so the normal world stays untouched and the client needs no change at all. The buff NPC stands on the exact town coordinates the old server used. Nobody asked for that detail, everybody noticed it.

![Mapas Especiais, Turn In and Cheffenia, live on the local server](/images/ragnaduds-events.mp4)

## A casino, played with zeny

Comodo has a casino hall in the original game, so I filled it. A hostess in Prontera takes you inside, and both floors now have working tables. Everything is played with zeny, the in game money, never with real money.

- **Blackjack** with a fresh six deck shoe every hand, a dealer who stands on all 17s, doubles and splits, and blackjack paying 3 to 2
- **Roulette** on two tables
- **Ten slot machines** sharing one progressive jackpot
- **A daily lottery** with tickets, where 70% of the sales go into the pot and the draw runs every evening
- **Jogo do Bicho**, Brazil's famous animal game. It started in 1892 as a raffle to keep a zoo in Rio de Janeiro open, and it has been illegal since the 1940s, yet you still find it on street corners all over the country. Twenty five animals each own four numbers, there are five draws a day, and you can bet on the animal or on the last two, three or all four digits of the winning number.

Every game is animated with art and sounds made by two small Python scripts, and the odds are tuned like the real thing, about 94% back on the slots, 97% on roulette and 99.5% on blackjack. The money is settled before the animation plays, so closing the game in the middle of a spin never eats a win.

![Roulette, slots, Jogo do Bicho, the lottery and blackjack, the real animation frames players see](/images/ragnaduds-casino.mp4)

## The website

A single static page, no framework, deliberately ugly in the way 2004 was ugly. Pixel font, CRT scanlines, the works.

- A **login page** with the same username and password as the game, and Caddy checks with the account portal before it serves any page
- **Live status** from the sidecar, whether each world is online and who is playing
- A **Hall of Fame** with the top ten by MVP kills and by PvP kills, the PvP counter coming from a small server script I wrote for it
- A **mini game** with my face on a knight sprite fighting an orc, ragdoll physics through matter.js
- A **collage** of my photo with game art on physics springs, backgrounds cut out with rembg, laid out with Pillow
- **Three languages**, EN, PT and DA, guessed from the browser and remembered

The Hall of Fame turned out to be the best thing on the whole site, not because it was hard, but because my friends now check it before they log in.

![Scrolling the site](/images/ragnaduds-website.mp4)

## Accounts, requests and email

The server is still friends only, but nobody has to message me for an account anymore. A small **account portal**, one Go binary with SQLite behind Caddy, takes care of it.

- Anyone can **request to join** on the website. They read the terms, confirm the project has no connection with Gravity, pick a username and leave a message if they want. The request then waits for me.
- Nothing is created until **I approve it**. Approving creates the game account on both servers at once and emails a link to choose a password. Rejecting can send a polite email as well.
- The same username and password open both the **website and the game**. Players can change their password from their account page, and a forgotten one gets a reset link that works once, for two hours.
- **Email** goes out over SMTP through the server's own Gmail account, and every message is also kept in an outbox page for me. Instead of a ping per request, I get one short daily summary when someone is waiting.

## Installers

Each download ships a Windows or a Linux installer. Both unpack the game, check every file against a manifest (sizes, plus the exe hash), confirm the client points at our server, test that the server answers, then create the shortcuts.

- **Windows**, PowerShell with WinForms, restyled to match the site. It has to stay ASCII only, because Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads scripts in the ANSI code page and a single accented character breaks the whole thing.
- **Linux**, Python with a GTK window that falls back to Tk, then zenity, then a plain terminal. Each install gets its own Wine prefix. It works on Fedora, which is what we run, and it knows Debian and Ubuntu need 32 bit Wine enabled first.
- The zips also carry a self hunting homunculus AI, so my friends do not need the external tools we all used as kids.

![The Linux installer halfway through unpacking the game](/images/ragnaduds-installer.jpg)

## Playing in the browser

Installing a 32 bit Windows game is still a small project of its own, so the newest piece is a **browser client**. Both worlds can be played straight from the website, behind the same login, with nothing to install.

- The client is **roBrowserLegacy**, an open source Ragnarok client written in JavaScript and WebGL, pinned to a tested commit with a few patches of my own on top.
- Browsers cannot open raw TCP connections, so a small **WebSocket proxy** runs next to it on the VM and forwards the game traffic to login, char and map, the same packets the desktop client sends. It only talks to our three game servers and only accepts pages from our own site.
- The game files are built from the **same downloads** my friends install, the same archives in the same order, the same music and the same item list, so both clients always match.
- Renewal needed two fixes. Its 2026 archives start with a different header, "Event Horizon" instead of "Master of Magic", so the file server had to learn to accept it, and the custom cash shop needed the same item preview fields as the desktop exe.

The browser does all the drawing. The server only moves files and game packets, exactly like it does for the installed game.

![Yeah, that's me in North Vietnam, close to China, ragnarokized](/images/ragnaduds-browser-login.jpg)

## Bugs worth telling

- **The server banned itself.** Before accounts existed, the char server kept dropping the map server, which reconnected many times per second, until rathena's anti flood guard banned our own container. Fixed by trusting the internal docker network.
- **A 5 GB installer crash.** PowerShell picked the integer overload of a Max call, and 5,140,330,802 bytes does not fit in an int. I reproduced the exact error message in a PowerShell container before touching the real installer, then moved it to doubles.
- **Commands did nothing.** rathena's commands aimed at other players start with a hash, but the 2026 client silently drops any chat line starting with one. So the command symbol became an exclamation mark.
- **Error loading data account settings.** Newer clients keep per account settings on a separate web service, and the translation pointed it at localhost. That is why rathena's web server shows up twice in the architecture diagram.

## What I learned

- **Legacy software is archaeology.** Version matching, byte patterns, reading archive formats nobody documents anymore. That was half the project.
- **Separating images from config** makes a tiny deployment feel professional. Releases, rollbacks, config changes, all of them are one boring command.
- **Test on the real target.** A 32 bit Lua runtime, Windows PowerShell 5.1, a clean Debian container. Almost every bug only showed itself there.
- **Nostalgia is a great project manager.** I would never have finished this for a client, but I finished it for friends who wanted to hunt Porings again.

Ragnarok Online is a trademark of Gravity Co., Ltd. This is a non commercial fan project for friends, not affiliated with Gravity, and no game files are distributed publicly.

::callout You are welcome to join [here](https://ragnaduds.duckdns.org/join)!

title: Personal Blog & Portfolio
description: This very site. A statically exported Next.js app with an interactive resume, a 3D travel globe, an activity tracker, physics banners and a JSON-driven blog.
content:
This is the source of the site you are looking at right now.

## Stack

Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4 and Bun as the runtime, exported to fully static HTML.

## Features

- Interactive resume with a career timeline and detail cards
- Portfolio tiles with per-project write-ups
- Blog with individual post pages
- A 3D travel globe built on three-globe
- A sports tracker with an activity log and pizza-earned charts
- Gravity and cursor-trail physics banners
- A contact form wired to a Cloudflare Worker with Turnstile

## Architecture

Content lives as JSON, is read through typed data modules, and feeds the App Router pages and their client components. Everything is prerendered to static files at build time.

::flow blog-architecture
